blocks.body:
By the prime number theorem, the gap after a prime $p$ near $x$ is about $\log x$ on average. The question is whether gaps far below average keep coming back, and in particular whether some fixed gap occurs infinitely often. The [[twin-primes|twin prime conjecture]] says the gap $2$ does. Until 2013 nobody could show that gaps below some fixed bound, even $10^{100}$, occur infinitely often.

In 2013 Yitang Zhang proved $\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n) < 7\times 10^7$. Within a year, James Maynard (and Terence Tao, independently) found a simpler and stronger sieve, and the Polymath8 project brought the bound down to
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n) \le 246.$$
This lesson explains the architecture: admissible tuples, a weighted count whose positivity forces two primes close together, and the role of the level of distribution from [[bombieri-vinogradov]].

blocks.title: Admissible tuple
blocks.body:
A set $\mathcal{H} = \{h_1 < h_2 < \dots < h_k\}$ of integers is admissible if for every prime $p$ the numbers $h_1,\dots,h_k$ miss at least one residue class mod $p$. Its diameter is $h_k - h_1$.

Admissibility is exactly the local condition that does not rule out all of $n+h_1,\dots,n+h_k$ being prime. Only primes $p \le k$ need checking, since $k$ numbers cannot cover more than $k$ classes.

blocks.title: Why tuples, and what the condition means
blocks.body:
If $\mathcal{H}$ is not admissible, some prime $p$ has every class mod $p$ hit by some $h_i$. Then for every $n$, one of $n+h_1,\dots,n+h_k$ is divisible by $p$. So all of them can be prime only when that one equals $p$, which happens for finitely many $n$. For example $\{0,2,4\}$ covers all classes mod $3$, and $n, n+2, n+4$ are all prime only for $n=3$.

The Hardy–Littlewood prime $k$-tuples conjecture says that for every admissible $\mathcal{H}$ there are infinitely many $n$ with all of $n+h_1,\dots,n+h_k$ prime. It is wide open, even for $\{0,2\}$. The bounded gaps theorems prove a much weaker statement that is still enough.

Weak tuples statement: for every admissible $\mathcal{H}$ with $k$ large enough, there are infinitely many $n$ such that at least two of $n+h_1,\dots,n+h_k$ are prime.

If two of them are prime, those two primes lie in an interval of length $h_k-h_1$, so some pair of consecutive primes differs by at most $h_k-h_1$. Bounded gaps then follows from two ingredients: a value of $k$ for which the weak statement is proved, and an admissible $k$-tuple of small diameter.

blocks.title: The GPY weighted count
blocks.body:
Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım (2005) found a way to detect two primes in a tuple. Take nonnegative weights $w(n)$ and look at
$$S = \sum_{N < n \le 2N}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n+h_i) - m\Bigr) w(n),$$
where $\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}$ is the indicator of the primes. If $S>0$, some $n$ in $(N,2N]$ has at least $m+1$ primes among $n+h_1,\dots,n+h_k$. The task is to choose $w$ so that $S$ can be computed asymptotically and turns out positive.

With $w(n)=1$ this fails badly. The sum of the indicators is about $kN/\log N$, which is much smaller than $mN$. The weights have to concentrate on the $n$ for which $\prod_i(n+h_i)$ has no small prime factors. That is what [[selberg-sieve]] weights do:
$$w(n) = \Bigl(\sum_{d \mid \prod_i (n+h_i)} \lambda_d\Bigr)^2, \qquad \lambda_d = 0 \text{ for } d > R.$$
Expanding the square, $\sum_n w(n)$ becomes a count of $n$ in residue classes modulo $[d,e] \le R^2$, which is elementary. In the sum $\sum_n \mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n+h_i)w(n)$ we have to count primes in residue classes modulo numbers up to $R^2$, with an error term summed over all those moduli. That is precisely a level of distribution statement. If the primes have level $\theta$, one can take $R^2 = N^{\theta-\varepsilon}$, so Bombieri–Vinogradov allows $R = N^{1/4-\varepsilon}$.

Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım used $\lambda_d = \mu(d)P(\log(R/d)/\log R)$ for a polynomial $P$. With $m=1$ they showed that any level $\theta > 1/2$ makes $S>0$ for $k$ large. Assuming the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture, they got infinitely many gaps of at most $16$. With $\theta = 1/2$, which is what is actually known, the method only just failed. It still gave $\liminf (p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log p_n = 0$.

blocks.title: Zhang, Maynard and Polymath
blocks.body:
Zhang got past the barrier from the other side, by improving the level. He proved a Bombieri–Vinogradov type estimate with level $\tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{584}$. It is restricted to squarefree moduli with no large prime factors, and to the particular residue classes the sieve produces. GPY weights can be truncated to such moduli at negligible cost. His proof uses deep bounds for exponential sums that come from Deligne's work. With $k = 3{,}500{,}000$ and an admissible tuple of that size, he obtained gaps below $7\times10^7$. The first Polymath8 project optimised his argument down to $4680$.

Maynard made the opposite move: keep level $1/2$ and improve the weights. He used a separate divisor for each shift:
$$w(n) = \Bigl(\sum_{d_i \mid n+h_i\ (1\le i\le k)} \lambda_{d_1,\dots,d_k}\Bigr)^2, \qquad \lambda_{d_1,\dots,d_k} \approx \Bigl(\prod_i \mu(d_i)\Bigr) F\Bigl(\frac{\log d_1}{\log R},\dots,\frac{\log d_k}{\log R}\Bigr),$$
where $F$ is a smooth function supported on the simplex $t_1+\dots+t_k \le 1$. The asymptotic evaluation of $S$ reduces to an optimisation problem for $F$. Let $M_k$ be the supremum, over admissible $F$, of
$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \int \bigl(\int F\, dt_i\bigr)^2 \, dt_1\cdots \widehat{dt_i}\cdots dt_k}{\int F^2\, dt_1\cdots dt_k}.$$
Maynard's criterion: if the primes have level $\theta$ and $M_k > 2m/\theta$, then every admissible $k$-tuple has infinitely many translates containing at least $m+1$ primes. He showed $M_k$ grows like $\log k$, so it eventually exceeds any bound. He also computed $M_{105} > 4$, which together with Bombieri–Vinogradov ($\theta=1/2$, $m=1$) gives gaps of at most $600$.

Polymath8b refined the variational problem, using a slightly larger support for $F$ and more careful error analysis. That made $k = 50$ enough, and an admissible $50$-tuple of diameter $246$ finished the job. On the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture Maynard had already obtained $12$ (improving the $16$ of Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım), and on a generalised form of the conjecture Polymath8b obtained $6$.

blocks.title: Bounded gaps (Zhang; Maynard; Polymath8b)
blocks.body:
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n) \le 246.$$
More generally (Maynard, Tao), for every $m \ge 1$, $\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+m}-p_n) < \infty$. Maynard's bound is $\ll m^3e^{4m}$.

blocks.title: What remains, and a 2026 report
blocks.body:
Why not $2$? Sieve weights are built from divisor conditions, and they cannot tell numbers with an odd number of prime factors from those with an even number. This is Selberg's parity problem. Polymath8b explained why their method cannot give a bound below $6$, even assuming generalised Elliott–Halberstam. The twin prime conjecture needs a genuinely new idea.

In August 2026 Axiom Math reported that its system AxiomProver had automatically produced a formal verification of the proof of the $246$ bound, and described it as the first of its kind. This is a claim reported by the developers. We describe nothing beyond that report.

blocks.title: Checking admissibility
blocks.body: Which of $\{0,2,6,8,12\}$ and $\{0,2,4,6\}$ are admissible? Then find the smallest diameter of an admissible $k$-tuple for $k = 2,\dots,7$.
blocks.solution:
Only primes $p \le k$ need checking. For $\{0,2,6,8,12\}$: mod $2$ every element is even, so class $1$ is missed. Mod $3$ the residues are $0,2,0,2,0$, so $1$ is missed. Mod $5$ they are $0,2,1,3,2$, so $4$ is missed. The tuple is admissible.

For $\{0,2,4,6\}$: mod $3$ the residues are $0,2,1,0$, which covers every class. Not admissible.

A computer search over tuples starting at $0$ gives minimal diameters $2, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20$ for $k=2,\dots,7$, attained for instance by $\{0,2\}$, $\{0,2,6\}$, $\{0,2,6,8\}$, $\{0,2,6,8,12\}$, $\{0,4,6,10,12,16\}$ and $\{0,2,6,8,12,18,20\}$. The minimal diameter grows roughly like $k\log k$, which is why the size of $k$ matters so much.

blocks.title: A cheap admissible tuple
blocks.body: Show that the first $k$ primes larger than $k$ form an admissible $k$-tuple. Compute the diameter this gives for $k=50$ and $k=105$, and compare with $246$ and $600$.
blocks.solution:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the first $k$ primes greater than $k$. For a prime $p \le k$, no element of $\mathcal{H}$ is divisible by $p$, since each element is a prime larger than $p$. So the class $0$ is missed. For $p > k$, the $k$ elements cannot cover $p$ classes. Hence $\mathcal{H}$ is admissible.

For $k=50$: $\pi(50) = 15$, so $\mathcal{H}$ runs from $p_{16} = 53$ to $p_{65} = 313$, and its diameter is $260$. For $k = 105$: $\pi(105)=27$, so $\mathcal H$ runs from $p_{28}=107$ to $p_{132}=743$, and its diameter is $636$. These are already close to the records $246$ and $600$. The records come from computer searches for denser admissible tuples.

blocks.title: Why weights are needed
blocks.body:
The positivity trick. Suppose that for every large $N$ there are weights $w(n) \ge 0$ with
$$\sum_{N<n\le 2N}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n+h_i) - m\Bigr)w(n) > 0.$$
Show that $\liminf_{j\to\infty}(p_{j+m}-p_j) \le h_k-h_1$. Then check numerically that $w \equiv 1$ is useless for $\mathcal H = \{0,2,6,8,12\}$, $m=1$, $N = 10^5$.
blocks.solution:
If every $n \in (N,2N]$ had at most $m$ primes among $n+h_i$, each summand would be $\le 0$, because $w(n)\ge0$. So the sum would be $\le 0$. Hence some $n_N \in (N,2N]$ has at least $m+1$ primes in $[n_N+h_1, n_N+h_k]$. Call them $q_1 < q_2 < \dots < q_{m+1}$ and write $q_1 = p_j$. There are at least $m$ primes after $p_j$ up to $q_{m+1}$, so $p_{j+m} \le q_{m+1}$ and $p_{j+m}-p_j \le q_{m+1}-q_1 \le h_k-h_1$. As $N \to \infty$ the $n_N$ are unbounded, which gives infinitely many such $j$.

With $w\equiv1$, $m=1$ and $N = 10^5$, a direct count gives
$$\sum_{10^5 < n \le 2\cdot 10^5}\Bigl(\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n+h) - 1\Bigr) = -58039 < 0.$$
Each shift contributes only about $N/\log N$ primes, so five shifts are far from enough. The sieve weights exist to make $w(n)$ large on the rare $n$ where the whole tuple is free of small prime factors.

blocks.body:
- Bounded gaps is not twin primes. The theorem gives some gap $\le 246$ infinitely often, without saying which one.
- The bound comes from the diameter of the tuple, not from $k$. The sieve says how large $k$ must be, and a separate combinatorial search supplies a tuple of small diameter.
- Level $1/2$ was not enough for GPY's one-dimensional weights. Maynard's weights are what make Bombieri–Vinogradov sufficient. Zhang's level beyond $1/2$ is a different route to the same goal.
- A liminf statement says such gaps occur infinitely often. On its own it says nothing about how often they occur.

The proof combines [[bombieri-vinogradov]] (level of distribution), [[selberg-sieve]] (the weights) and the combinatorics of [[prime-patterns|prime tuples]]. The obvious next target is the [[twin-primes|twin prime conjecture]], which is blocked by the parity problem of [[sieve-basics|sieve theory]]. Maynard's weights have since been used to find many primes in short intervals and to study large gaps between primes. The probabilistic view of primes in [[probabilistic-nt]] explains why the prime tuples conjecture should be true.

1. Decide whether $\{0,2,6,8,12,18\}$ is admissible.
2. Show that for $k\ge2$, every element of an admissible $k$-tuple has the same parity.
3. Using Maynard's criterion with $\theta = 1/2$, what lower bound on $M_k$ would show that infinitely often three primes lie in a tuple translate?
4. Assuming level $\theta$ for every $\theta<1$ (Elliott–Halberstam), what inequality on $M_k$ is needed for $m=1$?
